subject: Swaiman et al. (1968)
object: Swaiman et al. (1968) reported on late infantile acid maltase deficiency.

subject: Hudgson et al. (1968)
object: Hudgson et al. (1968) described adult myopathy caused by glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency.

subject: Engel (1970)
object: Engel (1970) reported studies in 4 adults with acid maltase deficiency. In these patients the syndrome could mimic muscular dystrophy or other myopathies.

subject: Angelini et al. (1972)
object: Angelini et al. (1972) reported abnormalities in fibroblasts cultured from patients with adult acid maltase deficiency.

subject: Askanas et al. (1976)
object: Askanas et al. (1976) established muscle tissue cultures from the biopsy of a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. Acid maltase (pH 4.0) activity, measured by maltose hydrolysis, was undetectable in both the cultured and the biopsied muscle. Acid phosphatase, another lysosomal enzyme, was increased in both.

subject: Askanas et al. (1976)
object: Askanas et al. (1976) reported that in a patient with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, light microscopy of biopsied muscle showed multiple vacuoles filled with acid-phosphatase-positive material. Electron microscopy showed abnormal accumulation of glycogen in membrane-bound sacs (secondary lysosomes), some of which also contained dark membranous or homogeneous material. The newly grown fibers of the cultured muscle showed the same abnormalities.

subject: Askanas et al. (1976)
object: Askanas et al. (1976) concluded that the reproduction of the morphologic and biochemical abnormalities in cultured muscle fibers supported the concept that adult-onset acid maltase deficiency is a biochemically distinct primary myopathy.

subject: Davis et al. (1976)
object: Davis et al. (1976) studied 8 patients with diaphragm weakness, suggested by inward movement of the abdominal wall on breathing in. Seven of the 8 had evidence of a generalized neuromuscular disorder. The change in pressure across the diaphragm during a maximum breath in was zero in 5 patients and 2 to 6 cm H2O in the other 3 (normal more than 25 cm H2O), indicating paralysis or severe weakness. Vital capacity was 30 to 65% of predicted when upright and typically fell by about half when lying down.

subject: Davis et al. (1976)
object: Davis et al. (1976) found alveolar hypoventilation in 5 patients when lying down and in 6 when asleep. Sleep worsened blood gases much more in these patients than in normal subjects. The patients breathed faster than age-matched controls and had an impaired ventilatory response to CO2. The hypoventilation was associated with disturbed sleep, morning headache and daytime fatigue.

subject: Davis et al. (1976)
object: Davis et al. (1976) found that fluoroscopy of the diaphragm gave misleading results in assessing diaphragm function. Patients could bring PCO2 to normal by deliberately breathing faster and deeper, so the authors stressed that voluntary breathing tests of this kind are unreliable measures of ventilatory reserve.

subject: Davis et al. (1976)
object: Davis et al. (1976) reported that patients with alveolar hypoventilation due to diaphragm paralysis improved in their symptoms when they used a cuirass respirator at night.

subject: Mehler and DiMauro (1977)
object: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) used a sensitive fluorometric assay and found residual acid maltase activity in muscle biopsies from 15 patients with late-onset acid maltase deficiency (mean 6.91% of normal; range 2.4 to 12.2%). They did not find this activity in biopsy or autopsy muscle from 3 patients with the infantile form. Electrophoresis, kinetic characteristics, and subcellular fractionation indicated that the residual activity was lysosomal acid maltase and not a contaminating neutral maltase isozyme.

subject: Mehler and DiMauro (1977)
object: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) found no correlation between the amount of residual acid maltase activity in muscle and either the clinical severity or the amount of glycogen accumulation in patients with late-onset acid maltase deficiency.

subject: Mehler and DiMauro (1977)
object: Mehler and DiMauro (1977) found acid maltase activity in muscle, liver, and especially leukocytes in late-onset but not infantile acid maltase deficiency. The two forms also did not occur together in the same family. From this, the authors suggested that the late-onset and infantile forms are genetically distinct.

subject: Beratis et al. (1978)
object: Beratis et al. (1978) purified acid alpha-glucosidase from normal fibroblasts and from fibroblasts of a patient with the adult form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency and found that the pH optimum, Michaelis constant, electrophoretic mobility in starch, thermal denaturation at pH 4.0 and 7.0, and inhibition by turanose, alpha-methylglucoside and trehalose were the same in the mutant and normal enzyme.

subject: Beratis et al. (1978)
object: Using monospecific antibodies against placental acid alpha-glucosidase, Beratis et al. (1978) found that cross-reacting material (CRM) in adult-form acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency fibroblasts appeared significantly reduced compared with normal cells or infantile-form cells, and that the immune complexes from adult-form cells retained enzyme activity, whereas those from infantile-form cells did not. They concluded that in the adult form the mutation causes a reduction in the amount of enzyme protein in the cells, whereas the infantile case resulted from a structural gene mutation producing a catalytically inactive, CRM-positive protein.

subject: Beratis et al. (1978)
object: Beratis et al. (1978) observed competition for antibody binding sites between normal enzyme and both infantile and adult mutant enzymes. They suggested that the infantile and adult forms of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency have different molecular defects: an inactive CRM-positive protein in the infantile form and a reduced amount of enzyme protein in the adult form.

subject: Sivak et al. (1981)
object: Sivak et al. (1981) reported a 51-year-old man with a 6-year history of gradually progressive exertional dyspnea. At first this was attributed to increasing age, but evaluation eventually showed diaphragmatic paralysis. Neurologic examination found only minimal weakness of the limb muscles. Exercise stress testing was needed to define the limits of his exercise tolerance.

subject: Sivak et al. (1981)
object: In the patient reported by Sivak et al. (1981), electromyographic studies suggested acid maltase deficiency. Electron microscopic and biochemical studies of a muscle biopsy confirmed the diagnosis.

subject: Francesconi and Auff (1982)
object: Francesconi and Auff (1982) reported cardiac arrhythmias in association with the adult form of type II glycogenosis (glycogen storage disease II).

subject: Slonim et al. (1983)
object: Slonim et al. (1983) treated a child with acid maltase deficiency and progressive muscle weakness with a high-protein diet for 12 months, which reversed the weakness and wasting, with improvement in muscle function, exercise tolerance, and growth.

subject: Slonim et al. (1983)
object: Slonim et al. (1983) observed a rapid fall in circulating branched chain amino acids after protein ingestion in a child with acid maltase deficiency, suggesting that increased net muscle protein catabolism may play a part in the pathogenesis of the progressive muscle weakness, in addition to intralysosomal glycogen accumulation and altered myofibrillar morphology.

subject: Beratis et al. (1983)
object: Beratis et al. (1983) studied cultured fibroblasts from 3 patients with the adult form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. In 2 strains, rocket immunoelectrophoresis showed less enzyme protein, and the reduction was directly proportional to the reduction in enzyme activity. The third adult-form strain had activity within the range of the infantile form, and no crossreacting material (CRM) could be identified. The authors concluded that there was molecular heterogeneity within the adult form as well as between the clinical forms.

subject: Beratis et al. (1983)
object: Beratis et al. (1983) found that of 9 fibroblast strains from patients with the infantile form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, 8 were CRM-negative and 1 was CRM-positive by both agar immunodiffusion and immunotitration. Apparent enzyme activity did not differ between the CRM-negative and CRM-positive infantile strains.

subject: Beratis et al. (1983)
object: Beratis et al. (1983) found that fibroblasts with phenotype 2 of acid alpha-glucosidase, which is considered a normal variant, had less enzyme protein and a reduced ability to cleave glycogen, but normal catalytic activity toward maltose. The authors stated that it remains unknown whether isozyme 2 homozygotes have enough enzyme deficiency to cause glycogen accumulation and a muscular dystrophy-like disease later in life.

subject: Matsuishi et al. (1984)
object: Matsuishi et al. (1984) studied 3 children with the childhood form of acid maltase deficiency (glycogenosis type II), including 2 sibs and 1 sporadic patient. Features included delayed developmental milestones and mild generalized muscle weakness. The authors considered nasal vocalization and an EMG finding of abnormal insertion voltage followed by pseudomyotonic discharge to be characteristic diagnostic findings for the childhood form.

subject: Matsuishi et al. (1984)
object: Matsuishi et al. (1984) found that neutral maltase activity was highest in the muscle biopsy from the patient with the least severe weakness among 3 children with childhood acid maltase deficiency, and suggested that this enzyme may play a role in reducing muscle involvement.

subject: Matsuishi et al. (1984)
object: Matsuishi et al. (1984) found selective type 2A fiber atrophy and type 2B fiber deficiency in affected muscles as common histochemical findings in the childhood form of acid maltase deficiency.

subject: Trend et al. (1985)
object: Trend et al. (1985) described 5 patients with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency whose initial pelvic girdle symptoms began late in the second or early in the third decade, followed some years later by signs of respiratory insufficiency. Typically the patients were tall, with weak and wasted paraspinal and gluteal muscles and lower limb weakness; all were orthopneic with marked diaphragmatic weakness.

subject: Trend et al. (1985)
object: Trend et al. (1985) found characteristic glycogen vacuoles in peripheral blood lymphocytes in all 5 patients, whereas muscle biopsy was characteristic in only 1 of 4 cases and showed minimal or nonspecific features in 3. Diagnosis was confirmed by acid maltase enzyme assay in muscle and cultured fibroblasts.

subject: Trend et al. (1985)
object: Trend et al. (1985) reported that long-term domiciliary ventilatory support (25 patient-years) using a rocking bed or intermittent positive pressure respiration via tracheostomy allowed all 5 patients to return to work, with clinical condition remaining stable.

subject: Byrne et al. (1986)
object: Byrne et al. (1986) described a family in which 7 members over 3 generations had a cardioskeletal myopathy. Muscle biopsy showed a vacuolar myopathy with excess free and intralysosomal glycogen storage, but acid maltase activity was normal. The authors called this the third report of lysosomal glycogen storage disease without acid maltase deficiency. They noted that, unusually among the glycogenoses, it had a dominant inheritance pattern.

subject: Byrne et al. (1986)
object: In the family reported by Byrne et al. (1986), biopsies showed a vacuolar myopathy with excessive free and intralysosomal glycogen storage in both skeletal and cardiac striated muscle. Postmortem studies in several patients showed changes of congestive cardiomyopathy with myocardial fibrosis.

subject: Byrne et al. (1986)
object: Byrne et al. (1986) found normal levels of acid maltase, phosphorylase and debrancher enzyme in skeletal muscle from 1 affected family member. Lysosomal enzyme screens and glycolytic enzyme levels were also normal.

subject: Margolis and Hill (1986)
object: Margolis and Hill (1986) described a 55-year-old man with adult acid maltase deficiency (AMD) and severe ventilatory muscle weakness. The authors noted that AMD in the adult is associated with progressive ventilatory muscle weakness and death from respiratory failure.

subject: Margolis and Hill (1986)
object: Margolis and Hill (1986) treated a 55-year-old man with adult AMD and severe ventilatory muscle weakness with a high-protein (1.6 g/kg), weight-reducing diet for 27 months, based on evidence that muscle catabolism may contribute to weakness. The therapy was associated with striking improvement in respiratory function, including measures of ventilatory muscle strength and endurance, and the authors suggested that high-protein dietary therapy may be useful in adults with AMD and respiratory insufficiency.

subject: Isaacs et al. (1986)
object: Isaacs et al. (1986) fully investigated an adult patient with lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. The patient was then given several forms of therapy and responded favorably to a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet.

subject: Isaacs et al. (1986)
object: Isaacs et al. (1986) discussed how acid maltase deficiency relates to muscle weakness and to glycogenosome formation, with or without accumulation of glycogen inside the muscle fibers.

subject: Makos et al. (1987)
object: Makos et al. (1987) reported 3 brothers, sons of healthy nonconsanguineous parents, who developed progressive proximal muscle weakness due to alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Each developed a fusiform basilar artery aneurysm; the aneurysm ruptured fatally in 2 of the brothers and was complicated by cerebellar infarction in the third.

subject: Makos et al. (1987)
object: In the brothers reported by Makos et al. (1987), postmortem examination showed severe vacuolation of skeletal muscle, liver, and vascular smooth muscle with accumulation of PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive material; in the surviving brother, similar glycogen deposition was shown in smooth muscle of the superficial temporal artery. The authors suggested that basilar artery aneurysm formation may be a consequence of alpha-glucosidase deficiency.

subject: Molho et al. (1987)
object: Molho et al. (1987) described 2 homozygote (identical) twin brothers who both developed bilateral paralysis of the diaphragm at age 50. Over 4 years of follow-up, no infectious, metabolic, degenerative, or proliferative disorder of the neuromuscular system and no thoracic disease that could explain the lesion was found. The authors concluded that it appeared to be an isolated lesion of genetic origin.

subject: Bashan et al. (1988)
object: Bashan et al. (1988) reported 18 patients with alpha-glucosidase deficiency diagnosed in Israel over 15 years. All were Palestinian Arabs except 2 sibs from a Jewish Iraqi family. All had the infantile type (Pompe disease) except 1 patient, who had the juvenile type.

subject: Bashan et al. (1988)
object: Among the patients reported by Bashan et al. (1988), muscle glycogen content ranged from 4 to 17% of wet weight. Muscle alpha-glucosidase activity was zero in 10 of 17 patients tested, and in the 7 with residual activity the highest value was 18% of normal. Leukocyte alpha-glucosidase activity was highly variable, so the authors judged leukocytes unsuitable for enzymatic diagnosis. pH profiles of muscle and leukocyte enzyme activity showed marked heterogeneity.

subject: Bashan et al. (1988)
object: Bashan et al. (1988) noted a high prevalence of alpha-glucosidase deficiency in the Arab population of Israel, a population with a high rate of consanguinity.

subject: Kretzschmar et al. (1990)
object: Kretzschmar et al. (1990) reported a patient with late-onset acid maltase deficiency who had marked liver and skeletal muscle involvement. Unlike other adult cases, the patient had CNS pathology: white matter areas that were hypodense on CT and hyperintense on MRI, and myelin changes ranging from focal demyelination to necrosis.

subject: Kretzschmar et al. (1990)
object: In their patient with late-onset acid maltase deficiency, Kretzschmar et al. (1990) found vacuolar degeneration of small and large cerebral arteries. Vacuoles in pericytes and arterial smooth muscle cells were partly filled with PAS-positive material. Electron microscopy showed lysosomal and free cytoplasmic glycogen in intimal smooth muscle cells of large cerebral arteries and in pericytes of arterioles and capillaries. Local glycogen accumulation was associated with severe cell damage and necrosis. The authors thought that this damage to the vessel walls caused the many small intracerebral aneurysms and suggested that the vascular pathology underlay the neuropathologic changes.

subject: Chancellor et al. (1991)
object: Chancellor et al. (1991) reported a 68-year-old man with acid maltase deficiency who presented with a myopathy and urinary incontinence brought on by exercise.

subject: Wokke et al. (1995)
object: Wokke et al. (1995) studied 16 patients from 11 families with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency and found that all were compound heterozygotes who carried the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion on one allele.

subject: Wokke et al. (1995)
object: In 7 of the 11 probands (64%) with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency, Wokke et al. (1995) found a deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2 of the GAA gene on the second allele, in trans with the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion.

subject: GAA deletion of a T at position 525 in exon 2
Wokke et al. (1995)
object: In 1 of the 11 probands (9%), Wokke et al. (1995) found a deletion of exon 18 of the GAA gene on the second allele, in trans with the IVS1(-13T-G) transversion.

subject: Wokke et al. (1995)
object: In the 16 patients with adult-onset acid maltase deficiency studied by Wokke et al. (1995), worsening of handicap was related to age, and the decline in vital capacity was related to how long the patient had had symptoms. Respiratory insufficiency was never the first manifestation. Muscle weakness progressed over a period of years.

subject: Wokke et al. (1995)
object: Wokke et al. (1995) found that serum creatine kinase activity and alpha-glucosidase activity in peripheral blood cells or muscle were helpful for diagnosis but did not have prognostic value.

subject: Wokke et al. (1995)
object: Wokke et al. (1995) concluded that the adult form of acid maltase deficiency appears to be fairly homogeneous both clinically and genetically. They suggested that reduced alpha-glucosidase activity is the final common pathway that leads to destruction of muscle fibers and progressive muscle weakness.

subject: Kroos et al. (1995)
object: Kroos et al. (1995) studied how often three common mutant alleles occurred in 121 patients with glycogen storage disease type II and which clinical phenotypes were associated with them.

subject: Bijvoet et al. (1998)
object: Bijvoet et al. (1998) generated a mouse model of GSDII (Pompe disease) by targeted disruption of the murine acid alpha-glucosidase gene (Gaa) in embryonic stem cells. Homozygous knockout (Gaa -/-) mice lacked Gaa mRNA and had a virtually complete acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Glycogen-containing lysosomes were detected soon after birth in liver, heart, and skeletal muscle cells. By 13 weeks of age, large focal glycogen deposits had formed, and vacuolar spaces stained positive for acid phosphatase, indicating lysosomal pathology.

subject: Bijvoet et al. (1998)
object: Bijvoet et al. (1998) found that male and female Gaa knockout mice were fertile. At 9 months of age, the oldest knockout mice still had no overt clinical symptoms, but their hearts were typically enlarged and their electrocardiograms were abnormal.

subject: Raben et al. (1998)
object: Raben et al. (1998) used gene targeting to disrupt the acid alpha-glucosidase gene in mice. Homozygous 6(neo)/6(neo) mice had no enzyme activity. Glycogen began to build up in cardiac and skeletal muscle lysosomes by 3 weeks of age and increased progressively, and by 3.5 weeks the mice had markedly reduced mobility and strength. The mice grew normally, reached adulthood and remained fertile. As in the human adult disease, older mice accumulated glycogen in the diaphragm, and by 8 to 9 months they developed obvious muscle wasting and a weak, waddling gait. The authors concluded that the model recapitulates critical features of both the infantile and adult forms of the disease.

subject: Raben et al. (1998)
object: Raben et al. (1998) also made a second Gaa mouse model with deletion of exon 6 (Delta6/Delta6). Like the exon 13 knockout, these mice kept normal strength and mobility up to 6.5 months of age, even though their biochemical and pathological changes could not be distinguished from those of the 6(neo)/6(neo) mice. The authors suggested that the genetic background of the mouse strains contributes to the differences among the three models.

subject: Martiniuk et al. (1998)
object: Martiniuk et al. (1998) determined the carrier frequency for glycogen storage disease type II in New York and estimated how many affected individuals are born with the disease.

subject: Ausems et al. (1999)
object: Ausems et al. (1999) performed a clinical, biochemical, and genetic study of 18 patients with adult-onset GSD II to assess the diagnostic value of laboratory tests. Measurement of GAA activity in muscle and histopathologic analysis of muscle tissue appeared to have no additional value when GAA activity in leukocytes was clearly deficient, and creatine kinase elevation was a sensitive marker of the disease. The authors formulated a diagnostic protocol.

subject: Laforêt et al. (2000)
object: Laforêt et al. (2000) studied 21 unrelated French patients with juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. Progressive muscle weakness began in adulthood in all but 1 patient, but 16 patients had mild, nonprogressive muscular symptoms that started in childhood. Eighteen patients had a similar pattern of pelvic girdle weakness, mostly affecting the glutei and thigh adductors. Eight patients had restrictive respiratory insufficiency with vital capacity below 60%, and in 2 patients respiratory failure was the first sign of disease.

subject: Laforêt et al. (2000)
object: Of the 21 French patients with juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency studied by Laforêt et al. (2000), 17 carried the IVS1-13T-G transversion in the GAA gene. One of these patients was homozygous for it; the others carried it as one allele. All patients except 1 were compound heterozygotes.

subject: Laforêt et al. (2000)
object: Laforêt et al. (2000) found both mutant GAA alleles in 10 of the 21 patients and detected 13 different mutations in total. They concluded that juvenile and adult acid maltase deficiency is genetically highly heterogeneous in the French population.

subject: Laforêt et al. (2000)
object: Laforêt et al. (2000) found no clear correlation between type of GAA mutation and phenotype in juvenile and adult-onset acid maltase deficiency. They suggested this pointed to a complex disease mechanism that needs further study.

subject: Lam et al. (2003)
object: Lam et al. (2003) described a 16-year-old Chinese patient with juvenile-onset glycogen storage disease type II (GSDII). His 13-year-old brother was asymptomatic despite carrying the same genotype. The authors concluded that intrafamilial phenotypic variation of juvenile-onset GSDII is ethnically diverse and suggested that other genes contribute to the phenotypic variability of GSDII.

subject: Lam et al. (2003)
object: In a 16-year-old Chinese patient with juvenile-onset GSDII, Lam et al. (2003) identified compound heterozygosity for 2 novel mutations in the acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) gene, P361L and R437C. His asymptomatic 13-year-old brother was also a compound heterozygote for the 2 mutations.

subject: Anneser et al. (2005)
object: Anneser et al. (2005) described a 30-year-old woman with late-onset Pompe disease. She had vascular involvement that resembled the atherosclerotic angiopathy of the elderly, which the authors considered an unusual phenotype.

subject: Hagemans et al. (2005)
object: Hagemans et al. (2005) used a questionnaire to collect information on 255 children and adults with Pompe disease. Disease severity was associated with how long patients had had the disease, not with their age. Earlier disease manifestation meant that patients became dependent on a wheelchair or ventilator earlier.

subject: Hagemans et al. (2005)
object: Hagemans et al. (2005) found that patients under 15 years of age included a subgroup whose disease was more severe and progressed more rapidly. The authors suggested that these patients need more intensive follow-up and early intervention, before irreversible damage occurs.

subject: Amartino et al. (2006)
object: Amartino et al. (2006) reported two clinical forms of glycogen storage disease type II in two generations of the same family.

subject: Montalvo et al. (2006)
object: Montalvo et al. (2006) performed complete molecular analysis of the GAA gene in 40 Italian patients with late-onset glycogen storage disease type II and identified 12 novel alleles. Missense mutations were functionally characterized by enzyme activity and protein processing in a human GAA-deficient cell line, and splicing mutations were studied by RT-PCR and in silico analysis. A complex allele carrying three different alterations in cis was also identified.

subject: Montalvo et al. (2006)
object: Montalvo et al. (2006) found that the c.-32-13T-G GAA mutation was the most frequent mutation among 40 Italian patients with late-onset GSDII, present in compound heterozygous state in 85% of patients (allele frequency 42.3%), as described in other late-onset Caucasian populations.

subject: Montalvo et al. (2006)
object: Montalvo et al. (2006) found the c.-32-13T-G mutation in association with the c.2237G-A (W746X) nonsense mutation in 9 of 40 Italian patients with late-onset GSDII, and discussed genotype-phenotype correlations with emphasis on this subgroup.

subject: Groen et al. (2006)
object: Groen et al. (2006) reported ptosis as a feature of late-onset glycogenosis type II (Pompe disease).

subject: Kallwass et al. (2007)
object: Kallwass et al. (2007) showed that a fluorometric assay of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) activity in dried blood spots efficiently detected patients with late-onset Pompe disease. The assay used acarbose, a highly selective alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, to remove interference from isoenzymes. The authors noted that late-onset patients are often misdiagnosed by conventional methods because other tissue types retain some GAA activity.

subject: Bembi et al. (2008)
object: Bembi et al. (2008) reviewed the management of glycogenosis type II. They described it as a multisystem disorder that requires care from a multidisciplinary team, including metabolic, cardiology, pulmonology, neurology, neuromuscular, respiratory, physical and occupational therapy, otolaryngology, speech, audiology, genetic counseling and dietetic specialists. They also discussed functional assessment, rehabilitation, nutritional management, genetic counseling, prenatal diagnosis, screening, and emerging therapeutic options.

subject: Bembi et al. (2008)
object: Bembi et al. (2008) described glycogenosis type II as a progressive, debilitating, and often fatal neuromuscular disorder that occurs as a continuum of clinical phenotypes. These phenotypes vary in organ involvement, age at onset, and severity.

subject: Bembi et al. (2008)
object: In a review, Bembi et al. (2008) stated that a clinical diagnosis of glycogenosis type II is confirmed by measuring GAA enzyme activity in blood samples, cultured fibroblasts, and muscle biopsies. Activity is virtually absent in infants and markedly reduced in juveniles and adults. The authors also reviewed the use of muscle imaging to evaluate muscle pathology.

subject: de Filippi et al. (2010)
object: de Filippi et al. (2010) studied the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) insertion/deletion polymorphism in 38 patients with late-onset Pompe disease, mean age 44.6 years. The genotype frequencies were similar to those of the general population: 16% II, 37% DD, and the rest ID. The 3 genotype groups did not differ in mean age, disease duration, Walton score, or other severity scores. However, the DD genotype was associated with earlier disease onset (P = 0.041), higher creatine kinase levels at diagnosis (P = 0.024), muscle pain (P = 0.014), and faster disease progression (P = 0.037). The authors suggested that the ACE polymorphism may modify the phenotype and prognosis of Pompe disease.

subject: Wang et al. (2011)
object: Wang et al. (2011), an ACMG work group, developed educational guidelines for diagnostic confirmation and management of presymptomatic individuals with lysosomal storage diseases, including glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease). These individuals were identified by newborn screening, by family-based testing after a proband was found, or by carrier testing in at-risk populations. The authors noted that the evidence in the literature was limited, so the recommendations should be considered expert opinion.

subject: Forsha et al. (2011)
object: Forsha et al. (2011) evaluated baseline ECGs and echocardiograms in 87 patients with late-onset Pompe disease (median age 44 years, 51% male, 94% Caucasian; median disease duration 15 years) enrolled in a randomized trial. Overall, 46% had 1 or more ECG or echocardiographic abnormalities: the most common ECG findings were left ventricular hypertrophy (12%) and short PR interval (10%, 90-120 ms); 7% had decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (41-54%), and 5% had elevated left ventricular mass index on echocardiogram, all in the mild range. Other findings included bundle branch block (4%), atrial enlargement (4%), and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (2 patients).

subject: Forsha et al. (2011)
object: Forsha et al. (2011) noted that severe ventricular hypertrophy classically associated with infantile Pompe disease was not observed in late-onset patients, and that ECG-defined left ventricular hypertrophy was not specific for increased left ventricular mass: of 10 patients with LVH on ECG, only 1 had elevated LV mass index on echocardiography. No differences were seen between patients with disease duration under vs at least 15 years; 3 of 5 (60%) patients with symptom onset before age 10 had abnormalities. The authors suggested the abnormalities may be related to Pompe disease or to comorbid conditions.

subject: Forsha et al. (2011)
object: Forsha et al. (2011) found that in a double-blind trial in which late-onset Pompe patients were randomized 2:1 to biweekly 20 mg/kg recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase or placebo for 78 weeks, no significant changes in ECG or echocardiographic parameters were associated with enzyme replacement therapy, and no significant cardiovascular safety concerns were identified. One patient with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome had an episode of supraventricular tachycardia after treatment, which was classified as serious and possibly related to the study medication.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) reviewed the records of 84 patients with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) carrying the c.-32-13T>G variant who were followed at Duke University Medical Center. Four patients (4.8%; 2 males and 2 females) were diagnosed clinically and had early-onset symptoms. All 4 were compound heterozygous for c.-32-13T>G and a second pathogenic variant. Symptom onset ranged from 10 days to 20 months and age at diagnosis from 10 to 26 months; median age at starting ERT was 23.5 months. The most common early features were delayed motor milestones with characteristic patterns of posture and movement (4/4), feeding difficulty (2/4) and sleep apnea (2/4). Cardiac involvement was absent.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) reported a Caucasian boy (patient 1) who presented at 5 months with delayed motor development, feeding and swallowing difficulty, easy fatigability, and snoring with likely apneic episodes. CK, ALT and AST were elevated. Muscle biopsy at 9 months showed PAS-positive vacuoles. GAA activity in fibroblasts was 4.35% of normal. At 15 months he had generalized hypotonia, head lag, myopathic facies and hypertrophied calves. EMG showed myotonic discharges, barium swallow showed penetration and aspiration, and polysomnography showed obstructive and central apneas. ECG and echocardiography were normal. He later developed coxa valga, mild ptosis and progressive thoracolumbar scoliosis that needed surgery at 12 years.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: In patient 1, a Caucasian boy with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) sequenced GAA and found the c.-32-13T>G splice variant together with c.525delT (p.Glu176Argfs*45).

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) described a Caucasian girl (patient 2), one of fraternal twins, who presented on day 10 of life with poor feeding, lethargy and vomiting. By 2 months she had breathing difficulty and sleep apneic episodes, and she also had hypotonia and developmental delay. Muscle biopsy at 14 months showed PAS-positive glycogen vacuoles, and blood GAA activity was low. She had failure to thrive, myopathic facies, scapular winging and neck flexor weakness, and walked at 17 months. Later problems included dysphagia needing a gastrostomy tube, gastroesophageal reflux, urinary retention, constipation, hypernasal voice and recurrent suspected aspiration pneumonia. Echocardiography and ECG were normal.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: In patient 2, a Caucasian girl with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.1827delC by molecular testing.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) described a Caucasian boy (patient 3) who could not sit unsupported or hold his head upright at 6 months. At 12 months he had an unsteady wide-based gait and frequent falls. At 23 months he had a weak cry, truncal hypotonia, proximal weakness, lordosis, scapular winging, scoliosis, a positive Gowers sign, and elevated CK, AST and ALT. Muscle biopsy showed PAS-positive glycogen storage. Later he developed mild ptosis, tongue weakness, scoliosis with a 40-degree Cobb angle, pectus excavatum, cramping, vomiting and diarrhea. His pulmonary function tests, ECG and echocardiography were normal.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: In patient 3, a Caucasian boy with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.2501_2502delCA (p.T834fs).

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) reported a Caucasian girl (patient 4) born preterm at 36 weeks who needed brief CPAP for apnea and bradycardia. Her motor milestones were delayed: she stood unsupported at 20 months and walked at 22 months. She had proximal weakness with a positive Gowers sign and a waddling gait, and spinal muscular atrophy testing was negative. Blood GAA activity was low and she was diagnosed at 26 months. She also had lumbar lordosis, winged scapulae, leg pain, snoring, apneic pauses and mild reversible obstructive airway disease. Cardiology evaluations were normal.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: In patient 4, a Caucasian girl with early-onset LOPD, Herbert et al. (2019) found the GAA variants c.-32-13T>G and c.118C>T by mutation analysis.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) noted that the second (non-IVS1) GAA variants in their 4 early-onset patients were nonsense or frameshift variants. However, c.525delT and c.1827delC were each found in 12 other patients in their LOPD cohort, all with adult-onset disease. The authors suggested that these genotype combinations are not enough to cause the early-onset phenotype. In patients 1 and 4, whose ACE genotypes were available, the unfavorable D/D genotype was absent. The authors proposed that other genetic and epigenetic modifiers might be involved.

subject: Herbert et al. (2019)
object: Herbert et al. (2019) found that all 4 early-onset LOPD patients improved on enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with alglucosidase alfa, but their gross motor function stayed below age level. All had residual weakness, including ptosis, lordosis, scoliosis, scapular winging, and trunk and limb weakness. Patient 1 had only partial improvement even at 40 mg/kg/week. Antibody titers stayed low in the 3 patients tested, and the authors suggested that patients with early onset have more rapid and severe progression.

subject: Korlimarla et al. (2020)
object: Korlimarla et al. (2020) assessed CNS involvement using brain MRI and developmental assessments in 14 children aged 6 to 18 years with Pompe disease on enzyme replacement therapy. Twelve had infantile Pompe disease and 2 had late-onset Pompe disease. The 2 children with late-onset Pompe disease had no white matter hyperintense foci and had high scores on most developmental assessments. In contrast, 10 of the 12 children with infantile disease had mild to severe white matter hyperintense foci.

subject: Jones et al. (2021)
object: Jones et al. (2021) assessed tongue structure and function in 10 treatment-naive patients with LOPD. They compared them with 30 patients with other acquired or hereditary myopathies and 30 controls with neuropathy, using manual and quantitative muscle testing and tongue ultrasound. Compared with the neuropathic controls, the LOPD patients had significantly different tongue strength, qualitative appearance, echointensity, and thickness. The authors concluded that tongue involvement in LOPD consists of weakness and sonographic abnormalities suggestive of fibrofatty replacement and atrophy.

subject: Jones et al. (2021)
object: Jones et al. (2021) found significantly lower quantitative tongue strength and significantly reduced tongue thickness on ultrasound in LOPD patients than in patients with other acquired or hereditary myopathies. They suggested that finding quantitative tongue weakness and/or atrophy may help distinguish LOPD from other myopathies. They also suggested that ultrasound is an effective point-of-care method for quantitative assessment of the tongue muscles.

subject: Huggins et al. (2022)
object: Huggins et al. (2022) systematically evaluated 20 infants aged 6 to 21 months with LOPD diagnosed by newborn screening. None of the infants had evidence of cardiomyopathy or cardiac rhythm disturbances. CK, AST, and ALT were elevated in 8 patients (40%), and Glc4 was elevated in 2 (10%). All patients showed postural and kinematic concerns. Three patients (17%) scored below the 10th percentile on the Alberta Infant Motor Scale. Speech-language assessments were normal in all patients, and 9 (45%) had mild feeding or swallowing abnormalities. The authors concluded that phenotype varied widely and that careful physical therapy evaluation was needed to detect subtle musculoskeletal signs of early muscle involvement.

subject: Huggins et al. (2022)
object: In the 20 infants with LOPD identified by newborn screening, Huggins et al. (2022) found 4 who were homozygous for the IVS1 splice site variant c.-32-13T>G in the GAA gene. Fourteen were compound heterozygous for this variant, and 2 did not carry it.

subject: Huggins et al. (2022)
object: Huggins et al. (2022) studied children with LOPD diagnosed through newborn screening. Because of the high variability they found, they recommended careful physical therapy evaluation and close monitoring for symptom progression.
